issues.legal_issue: Occupiers who bear an appreciable share of a municipal property tax are entitled to participate in the valuation and assessment process.
material_facts: The tax was apportioned between the owner and tenants, sub-tenants, or occupiers, who could bear an appreciable part of the consolidated rate and, in some cases, the surcharge.
The statutory scheme provided for public and written notices, returns, objections, and hearings in the valuation and assessment process.
issues.conclusion: Tenants, sub-tenants, and occupiers liable for a share of the tax are entitled to participate in valuation and assessment, including through written notices and consideration of returns they submit.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 181, 184, and 186 provide for returns, notice, and objections; Section 178(6) provides for information about apportionment. Since occupiers bear an appreciable tax burden, they must have an effective opportunity to participate. The Court relied on Assistant General Manager, Central Bank of India v. Commissioner, Municipal Corporation, which recognised a tenant's standing to object and appeal where directly affected by an assessment.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment_procee: The proceeding concerns valuation or assessment of property for municipal taxation.
predicates.occupier_bears_appreciable_tax_share: A tenant, sub-tenant, or other occupier is liable to bear an appreciable share of the tax.

issues.definition: When an occupier bears an appreciable share of municipal property tax in an assessment proceeding, the occupier is entitled to participate in the assessment process.

issues.legal_issue: Omission or non-service of assessment notices does not invalidate a municipal property tax assessment unless the omission causes serious prejudice.
material_facts: The statutory process contemplated public and written notices to owners, lessees, sub-lessees, and occupiers.
The Court recognised practical difficulties in giving individual notices to every occupant of multi-storeyed buildings.
The Court held that an aggrieved person could challenge an assessment where lack of notice caused serious prejudice.
issues.conclusion: Non-issuance or non-service of notices does not necessarily invalidate an assessment, reassessment, or amendment unless serious prejudice is established.
issues.legal_principle: The notice requirements must be followed, but a failure to issue or serve notices on all concerned persons does not automatically invalidate the proceedings. The controlling consideration is whether the omission caused serious prejudice to the aggrieved person.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment_procee: The proceeding concerns assessment, reassessment, or amendment of municipal property tax.
predicates.assessment_notice_omitted: A public notice was not issued or a written notice was not served on a concerned person.
predicates.serious_prejudice_established: The aggrieved person established that the notice omission caused serious prejudice.

issues.definition: An assessment proceeding is not invalidated for an omitted notice when the proceeding concerns municipal property tax and the omission is not shown to have caused serious prejudice.

issues.legal_issue: An occupier liable for only an apportioned share of municipal property tax may appeal after depositing that share rather than the tax assessed on the entire property.
material_facts: Tenants, sub-tenants, and occupiers were liable for apportioned shares of the consolidated rate and, where applicable, the surcharge.
The appeal provision required a deposit of the consolidated rate but, read literally, could require an occupier of only part of a building to deposit the tax assessed on the whole building.
The assessment and demand information made the amount apportioned to each person ascertainable.
issues.conclusion: A tenant, sub-tenant, or occupier liable for a portion of the tax has a right of appeal upon depositing the portion assessed as payable by that person.
issues.legal_principle: Section 189(5) and (6), read down harmoniously with the scheme of apportionment, allows an appeal upon deposit of the appellant's apportioned liability, not the tax assessed on the whole building. Reading down is a tool of harmonious construction used to make a provision workable and fulfil the statute's purpose, but cannot contradict clear statutory language. The Court relied on BR Enterprises v. State of U.P. for that principle and distinguished Assistant General Manager, Central Bank of India v. Commissioner, Municipal Corporation because the scheme there lacked the relevant features of this scheme.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_appeal_proceeding: The proceeding is an appeal by a person affected by a municipal property tax assessment.
predicates.appellant_liable_for_apportioned_share: The appellant is liable for only an apportioned share of the tax on the property.
predicates.whole_property_deposit_exceeds_appellant: The tax assessed on the whole property exceeds the amount apportioned to the appellant.

issues.definition: In a municipal property tax appeal, a person liable for an apportioned share may appeal by depositing that person's share rather than the greater amount assessed on the whole property.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord may recover from an occupier the tax share paid on the occupier's behalf as rent, with the related tenancy-law remedies applying to that recovery.
material_facts: The landlord was primarily liable to the Corporation for the consolidated rate and could be required to pay the tax share apportioned to an occupier.
The statute gave the landlord the same rights and remedies for recovery of that share as if it were rent payable by the occupier.
The appellants argued that treating tax as rent could expose an occupier to tenancy-law recovery or eviction proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The statutory treatment of the occupier's tax share as rent for recovery is valid; the tax share may be recovered through the applicable rent-recovery mechanisms.
issues.legal_principle: Section 231 creates a fiction treating the tax share paid by the landlord on behalf of the occupier as rent for recovery. The fiction must be taken to its logical conclusion, and the municipal legislation and tenancy legislation are to be read harmoniously. The Court relied on Puspa Sen Gupta v. Susma Ghose for the proposition that rent is a compendious expression that may include taxes and other charges. The fiction facilitates recovery and does not itself make the tax share anything other than a recovery claim governed by the applicable legal remedies.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_recovery_proceedi: The proceeding concerns recovery of municipal property tax from an occupier through the landlord.
predicates.landlord_paid_occupier_tax_share: The landlord paid a tax share that was apportioned to the occupier.
predicates.statute_authorizes_rent_like_recovery: The governing law gives the landlord rent-like rights and remedies to recover that share.

issues.definition: Where a landlord pays an occupier's tax share and the law authorizes rent-like recovery, the landlord may recover that share as rent.

issues.legal_issue: A dispute between landlord and tenant about rent does not require municipal authorities to postpone property tax assessment.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the Corporation could attach rent based on the landlord's asserted rent even where the tenant disputed that amount.
The Court held that a tenant could raise the rent dispute before the competent municipal authority during valuation and assessment and could also seek adjudication by a competent court.
issues.conclusion: Municipal authorities need not wait for a separate forum to resolve a rent dispute before finalising assessment; the tenant may raise the dispute in the assessment process and seek adjudication through the competent court.
issues.legal_principle: A rent dispute does not prevent municipal authorities from completing an assessment. The tenant may object to the asserted rent before the competent authority under the municipal scheme and pursue adjudication by a competent court.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment_procee: The proceeding concerns valuation or assessment of municipal property tax.
predicates.landlord_tenant_rent_dispute: The landlord and tenant dispute the rent relevant to the assessment or recovery.
predicates.tenant_can_raise_rent_objection: The tenant can raise the rent dispute before the competent authority in the assessment process.

issues.definition: When a rent dispute can be raised in the municipal assessment process, the assessment need not await its resolution in a separate proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A property tax scheme is not invalid merely because the occupier bears more of the tax burden than the landlord.
material_facts: The landlord's liability was limited by reference to actual rent received, while the occupier could bear tax calculated by reference to the property's annual letting value.
The Corporation relied on the use of premises for commercial and non-residential purposes and the occupiers' actual use of civic amenities, despite comparatively low rents received by landlords.
The occupiers could derive substantial benefit or income from the premises while the landlord's rent was constrained.
issues.conclusion: The greater tax burden on tenants, sub-tenants, or occupiers than on landlords is not, by itself, a legitimate ground to invalidate the tax provisions.
issues.legal_principle: In assessing the validity of the apportionment, the Court considered the actual and notional rental values, the occupier's use of the property, and the need to fund municipal services. A comparatively greater burden on an occupier who uses the premises for commercial or non-residential purposes is not inherently inequitable or unconstitutional.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_scheme_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a municipal property tax scheme.
predicates.landlord_tax_based_on_actual_rent: The landlord's tax liability is limited by reference to the rent actually received.
predicates.occupier_tax_reflects_property_use: The occupier's tax liability reflects the property's letting value or the occupier's commercial or non-residential use.

issues.definition: A municipal tax scheme is not invalid solely because an occupier bears more tax than a landlord where their liabilities reflect actual rent and the property's use.

issues.legal_issue: Different tenancy-law coverage of rented premises does not make a uniform municipal tax apportionment scheme discriminatory.
material_facts: Some rented premises were covered by tenancy legislation while others, including premises with higher rents, were not.

The municipal scheme uniformly apportioned tax by reference to actual and notional rental value, limited the landlord's liability by actual rent, and permitted recovery of the occupier's share through the landlord.
The tax share was treated as rent only for the limited purpose of recovery.
issues.conclusion: The difference in tenancy-law coverage does not create discrimination in the application of the municipal tax scheme between tenants of the different categories of premises.
issues.legal_principle: The municipal scheme applied a uniform method of tax apportionment to tenants regardless of whether tenancy legislation covered their premises. The limited treatment of a tax share as rent for recovery does not create a different municipal tax liability between those categories.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_scheme_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a municipal property tax scheme.
predicates.tenancy_law_covers_only_some_rented_prem: Tenancy legislation applies to some rented premises but not to others.
predicates.tax_apportionment_applies_uniformly: The municipal scheme apportions tax using the same method for tenants across both categories of premises.

issues.definition: Different tenancy-law coverage does not make a municipal tax scheme discriminatory when the same tax-apportionment method applies to tenants in both categories.
